note: Six strips from a Middle Dutch book of saints' legends in numbered sections (red rubrics Prima / Secunda / [Ter]cia ...ctio, probably lectio; a red number lxxxx). One strip has the Petronilla legend and another probably the Nicholas story of the poor nobleman's daughters. Both passages were compared on page images with the Southern (Delft 1482 Passionael) and Northern (Gent UB HS.0123) translations of the Legenda aurea and match neither, so the text is another version, likely office lessons; the containing work was not found.

identification: Small-format book arranged by Sundays after Pentecost ('Dominica xiiij, Mattheus', Mt 6:24; Dominica xi, Mc 7); sermons or postil, work unidentified
note: The four spine strips come from a small 14th-century book arranged by the Sundays after Pentecost: red rubrics "Do(minica) xj. M[ar.]" (F4) and "Do(minica) xiiij. Math." (F3) can be read, the latter followed by "[Nemo potest] duobus dominis servire" (Mt 6:24), which matches Roman/Franciscan pericope numbering and the catalogue's Mc 7:32 on F4. The suggested reading "dist. xiiij ... magister" (Sentences commentary) does not hold. The body text is out of focus in every photograph, so the work (sermons, postil or thematic outlines) is not identified; better photographs of F3 and F4 are needed.

identification: Besides the catalogued Isidore, Etymologiae I: five lines before De soloecismo that end De barbarismo with matter on conlisio and hiatus not in Isidore's text; source unidentified
note: The unidentified text is five lines at the top of fol. 1r, the end of a chapter on barbarism that replaces or expands Isidore's Etym. 1.32.8-9: an L-alliteration example, conlisiones with Virgil (read as Aen. 5.866) and a second example, and the sentence "Hiatus vero et conlisiones per vocales et consonantes fiunt". It is not the standard Isidore text, not Julian of Toledo, and not in Zofingen Pa 32 or St. Gallen 237, which were read on the page; Spevak's 2017 study of additions to book I reports nothing at this point, and Pompeius offers parallels of content only. The leaf may come from a school copy of book I (Ars Isidori) with added Donatus-commentary material; that is a lead, not a finding.

identification: Trimmed leaf in a small faint hand; no secure word sequence at the published resolution
note: The strip occupies only about 650 x 1650 pixels of each published image, with lines 12-15 px high; contrast enhancement in three treatments on both faces gave letter groups but no readable word sequence, so no search was possible. The limit is image resolution as much as abrasion; a higher-resolution capture from the Erfgoedbibliotheek would reopen it.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 17/7
identification: Rules of consequence on the integral whole; one rule ('a toto integrali distributo ad partem distributam') is closely parallel to Ockham, Summa logicae III-3 c. 3, the only text found with it; dependence not shown; work unidentified
note: The recto has the rule "Alia regula est a toto [integrali] distributo ad partem distributam est consequentia bona", a close parallel in shortened wording to Ockham, Summa logicae III-3, c. 3; the neighbouring lines do not follow Ockham's text. Albert of Saxony, Buridan with Dorp, the pseudo-Ockham Elementarium and Tractatus minor, Burley and Greve were compared and do not have the distributed rule; Marsilius and Strode were not reached. One shared rule with differing context and untested alternatives is a promising connection, not shown dependence; the work is not identified.

identification: Avicenna, Canon medicinae (Latin of Gerard of Cremona), III, fen 3, tract. 1, end of ch. 1 (De anatomia oculi) and rubric of ch. 2
note: Strip A keeps only the first or last few letters of the bottom 24 lines of two columns; 22 of 24 line ends on one side and all 24 line beginnings on the other, ending in the rubric [com]plexionum eius, stand in the order and spacing of Canon III.3.1.1-2 in the Padua 1479 print. A research reader compared them with the print's page images; the coordinator read the first eleven line beginnings of canvas 0 on the native image and lines 1-19 of that side on the print's pages. One doubtful reading (similiter for the print's simile) could not be decided; only one print was compared and the attribution of the translation to Gerard of Cremona is the conventional one, not checked. Strip B carries only a marginal scheme. The catalogue's 'probably a treatise on optics' is corrected to medical anatomy of the eye.

catalogue_title: Mortuary roll asking for prayers for John, monk and cantor at an unidentified abbey
identification: Mortuary roll with the letter printed as Codex Dunensis no. 276 (already in the catalogue), here naming John, cantor, priest and professed monk; the sending house is named in neither witness and remains unidentified
note: The roll carries the same letter as Codex Dunensis no. 276, as the catalogue says, in a fuller form that names the deceased as John, cantor, priest and professed monk 'of our aforesaid monastery'; the line that named the monastery is lost and the dorse is blank. The printed letter has the sender removed as well, so no house is named in either witness. The encyclicals of St Bavo's Abbey, Ghent (roll of abbot Gerelmus, 1336, read on the image) share four or five formulae with it inside a different composition, and where the two differ the roll follows the Codex Dunensis wording, so St Bavo's is no stronger a candidate than another Flemish house. Nothing in the wording decides between Benedictines and Cistercians.

identification: Liturgical psalter (Gallican), Psalm 68:15-22 on 367a-1: 1v; the other three faces are not placed
note: On the face 367a-1: 1v ten line beginnings read in order as Psalm 68:15-22, with a two-line red initial at v. 17 where the Benedictine office divides the psalm for Wednesday Matins. A research reader reread the lines on the image and compared them with a transcription of the Stuttgart Gallican text; no page image of an edition or medieval psalter was used, and the monastic division was checked only in a modern table. Where it can be told the reading has the Clementine form 'respice in [me]'. The other three faces give word shapes only; Ps 67:20-24, the opening of Ps 59 under 'fer. iiij' (title too long for the lines, unresolved) and Ps 61:11 onward are leads, not placements. The identification is of the Psalm 68 face alone; book type is inferred and monastic use remains provisional.

identification: Hostiensis (Henricus de Segusio), Lectura in Decretales Gregorii IX, on X 3.30.33-34 (De decimis: end of c. Cum non sit in homine, and c. Nuper abbates)
note: Twenty of the 21 surviving line ends and line beginnings on both faces agree in wording and order with Hostiensis's Lectura through nine successive lemmata. A research reader compared both faces on the published images with the page image of the Strasbourg 1512 edition (vol. 2, fol. 114r) and with text-recognition snippets of the Venice 1581 edition. Johannes Andreae's Novella rewords these comments and cites Hostiensis by name at the points the fragment preserves; it was excluded on the page image of the Venice 1581 edition (vol. 3, leaves 146v-147r) for the comments on Per censuram ecclesiasticam, De iure and Nisi cum ipsis. The ordinary gloss was excluded on a page image. No difference of wording in the surviving words; about one line's worth of text between lines 6 and 7 of the first face was probably absent from the manuscript (inferred from spacing), and the first line of the second face is cut through and unplaced. No manuscript of the Lectura was compared.

catalogue_title: Unidentified | Different types of scripts on parchment
identification: Greek bifolium in faded abbreviated cursive with pen trials; single words only; not part of the host manuscript's text
note: The bifolium's text stays unidentified: its two inner pages are in a faded, heavily abbreviated cursive from which only single words could be read, and the back carries alphabet pen trials over rubbed small script. It is not part of the host text and is in different hands. The page with the majuscule line belongs to the host manuscript, not the fragment, and is the end of Climacus's Ad Pastorem with the explicit "Τέλος σὺν Θεῷ τοῦ Κλίμακος", checked against PG 88 through search snippets only.

identification: Chain of authorities: pseudo-Bernard, Meditationes III.8 (abridged; contact already in the catalogue), 1 Peter 1:18 and Ecclesiasticus 6:15; the compiling work unidentified (not the Manipulus florum or the Viridarium consolationis)
note: Partial. Strip 4 quotes pseudo-Bernard, Meditationes III, 8 in sequence (already noted by the catalogue) but abridged and introduced by 1 Peter 1, 18; strip 1 carries Ecclesiasticus 6, 15 in a chain of biblical authorities ending at a rubric. The fragment is therefore from a compilation or treatise of authorities, not from the Meditationes; the compiling work was not found. Only line beginnings and ends are visible, so no further search text is available without access to the hidden parts.

identification: Scholastic text on alteration, local motion and substantial form, probably on De generatione et corruptione I; not the questions of Albert of Saxony or Marsilius of Inghen on augmentation, nor Giles of Rome's exposition; work unidentified
note: Not identified. The legible words (alteration, local motion, substantial form, probably augmentation and mixtion) suggest a commentary or questions on De generatione et corruptione I, not the Physics as the catalogue guesses. Albert of Saxony's and Marsilius of Inghen's question on augmentation and Giles of Rome's exposition of the mixtion chapter were read in the 1567 Venice print and do not fit. Their mixtion questions, and Buridan and Oresme, are still untested.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
identification: Paper snippets from at least three books: an allegory of the six days and the seventh, a comment on De profundis, a passage on priestly power; no source found
note: Ten photographed paper snippets from at least three different books; only pieces [1], [3] and [4] carry connected Latin prose. Piece [4] has an allegory of the six days and the seventh day (creation, redemption, rest); piece [1] comments on "De profundis clamavi"; piece [3] concerns priestly power and remission. Phrase searches in Corpus Corporum, Google Books, Internet Archive and MDZ found no match, so the record stays unidentified.

identification: Scholastic text on the differences of the Old and New Law, close in matter to Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II q. 91 a. 5 but not that text; work unidentified
note: The 37 Ghent strips each keep only 4-9 letters a line. They come from a 14th-century scholastic text on the Old and New Law (lex vetus / lex nova, testamentum, moral and ceremonial precepts, Augustine cited), close in matter to Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II q. 91 a. 5 and q. 107 a. 1, but not the text of those articles. The work is not identified; the strips were not reassembled.

identification: One trimmed line a face; no secure word at the published size
note: Unidentified. One trimmed line per face was reread at native size with contrast stretching; it gives word shapes such as "viueret(?)" and "faceret(?)" but no secure connected phrase, and no rubric, running title or legal citation is visible. No candidate was searched or tested; a better image of the cut edges is the precondition for further work.

identification: Cover leaf abraded beyond reading in the published images
note: The cover leaf of MdS 27 Aa 19 is abraded beyond reading in the published images; only five line-beginnings beside a blue initial M are visible. No text could be searched, and the record stays unidentified. The pale spine strip carries Roman-law allegation notes and belongs to the separate reinforcement (compare sibling F-jnye), not to the catalogued bifolium.

identification: Faded leaf with red section references, perhaps to Exodus 21 and 23; no connected text legible
note: Only one face of one strip carries legible ink, and even with flat-field and channel enhancement no connected phrase could be read. The red notes after the underlined blocks are best read as biblical references ("Exod. xxj", "Exod. xxiij", and ".xij." on the other leaf), which would make the underlined text quotations from Exodus followed by comment; the first-pass reading "Error" is withdrawn. Both readings rest on four worn red letters and neither was tested against a text. The record stays unidentified; better imaging is the realistic next step.

institution: Faido, Biblioteca del Convento dei Frati Cappuccini
identification: Latin Sunday sermon cycle, not a liturgical book: end of a Septuagesima sermon ('Ideo officium incipit: Circumde[derunt]') and start of a Sexagesima sermon ('Exiit qui seminat etc. Super'), matching nos. 12-13 of an anonymous cycle in Schneyer, Repertorium 8, pp. 412-413 (Kremsmünster, Stiftsbibliothek, CC 273); no manuscript of the cycle compared
note: Not a liturgical book: the strips come from a Latin Sunday sermon cycle. One column shows "...vio. Ideo officium incipit: Circumde[derunt]" followed by a red initial and "Exiit qui seminat etc. Super", which matches the end of the Septuagesima sermon and the start of the Sexagesima sermon in an anonymous cycle in Schneyer 8, pp. 412-413 (Kremsmünster 273, 14th c.). Schneyer was seen only in snippets, and the one witness for this part of the cycle is not online (vHMML microfilm, on-site or by order), so no manuscript was compared and the result stays partial. The catalogue's Ps 76 and James 5:16 are quotations inside the sermons; its "Luke 5:16" is a slip for James.

identification: Psalm 63:2-6 on strip F4, as the catalogue's linked description already says; kind of psalter open; strip F3 unidentified
note: The catalogue's linked description already identifies strip F4 as Psalm 63:2-6, in spite of the record title; this was confirmed on the image (a timore ini / [Pr]otexisti / -ntium a mult- / Qui / S), with a steady 28-32 letters a line and nothing inserted between verses. The book is a psalter of undetermined kind (run-on verses with one-line red initials); psalter or breviary cannot be decided. Strip F3 shows only two letters a line and stays unidentified.

identification: Scholastic text quoting Augustine, De Trinitate XV.27 in abridged form (quotation already in the catalogue); not Aquinas's Scriptum at the distinctions tested; work unidentified
note: The legible half-lines are scholastic in vocabulary (philosophus, motus, naturale, dilectio, cognitio), so the catalogue's 'religious text' is a scholastic theological or philosophical text; it quotes Augustine, De Trinitate XV.27, in abridged form, which the catalogue had noted. Thomas Aquinas's commentary on the Sentences was compared at I d. 3, II d. 30-33 and III d. 27-32 (transcription) and has neither the quotation nor the half-lines. Other commentaries on the Sentences were not reached; the heading 'XXX' could not be seen in the images.

identification: Middle Dutch narrative prose, perhaps a saint's legend or miracle; no source found
note: Five small binding strips of Middle Dutch narrative prose, about twenty letters a line. All faces were read; the legible phrases ('vielen si neder ende dancten gode', 'sieken of gequets-', 'godliker mogentheit') were found in sequence in no text of the Corpus Middelnederlands, Google Books or the Internet Archive. A name ending in -us on one strip may be Franciscus or Dominicus, which with the context suggests a saint's legend or miracle; the Middle Dutch legend collections are not searchable and were not compared.

identification: Geert Grote, Getijdenboek (Middle Dutch hours), Hours of the Eternal Wisdom, Compline: end of hymn Ihesus regniert in den vreden and antiphon O gloriose coninc onder dinen heilighen (Van Wijk 1940, p. 111)
note: Two strips and a scrap are parts of one leaf: the recto line ends and the verso line beginnings on the strips, with the opposite ends of the same lines on the scrap, agree in wording and order with the hymn and Nunc dimittis antiphon of Compline of the Wisdom Hours in Van Wijk's edition, p. 111. A research reader reread strips verso lines 2-10, recto lines 1-6 and the scrap on enlargements against the DBNL transcription of the edition; the printed page was not seen. Differences are small (bis altoes without die, dinen for dine, waerdighe- for verwerdighen, weter for weder); verso line 8 and recto lines 1, 4-5 are rubbed and only compatible. Other Middle Dutch versions of Suso's Cursus were not compared, a prayer book with only the Wisdom Hours is not excluded, and the third strip (canvases 2-3) is illegible and unplaced.

institution: Elbląg, Biblioteka Elbląska im. C. Norwida
identification: Middle Dutch devotional text in the first person with a rubric and red initial, six to nine letters a line; no source found
note: Five spine-lining strips still in place; one is a scrap of painted border, four carry six to nine letters from each of about ten lines of a Middle Dutch text in the first person with a rubric and a red initial. Strips 1, 3 and 4 were read and strip 5 is illegible; no source was found in the Corpus Middelnederlands. A reading of strip 1 as the opening of Psalm 13 or 52 ('Die sot') does not fit the neighbouring line beginnings.

identification: One exposed line of a noted chant ('...arni si...'); the rest is under the pastedown
note: Only "[...]arni si[...]" and a red initial A are exposed along the joint; the rest of the strip is under the pastedown. All eight images were checked and none shows more. Cantus Index and the Cantus Database (tools/cantus.py, standard texts and manuscript readings, substring) give one chant with the sequence: the Agnes antiphon Beata Agnes in medio flammarum (Cantus ID 001559) as written in Vienna Cod. 1890, 'et carni spurcitias'. It does not fit: the letter after long s is a minim with no descender, so the fragment cannot read 'sp'. No chant can be named; the fragment stays unidentified until the pastedown is lifted or imaged through.

identification: Spine line 'item dauid rex apte dicitur', a phrase found only in Sedulius Scottus, In Matthaeum, on Mt 1:6; one phrase, no second passage legible; work unidentified
note: The spine line reads 'item dauid rex apte dicitur', as the catalogue says; nothing else on the leaf could be read with confidence. That phrase was found only in Sedulius Scottus's commentary on Matthew at Mt 1:6 (ed. Loefstedt, p. 25, seen in snippets), so the leaf is probably from a commentary on the genealogy in Matthew. A test of the neighbouring letter groups against Sedulius's sentences gave no confirmation, his Hiberno-Latin sources could not be consulted, and one phrase does not identify the work.

identification: Small cursive not resolved by the published image (about 13 pixels a millimetre)
note: Not identified. The published images give about 13 pixels per millimetre, too little to read this small cursive, and contrast enhancement did not help. No phrase could be read securely, so no search was run. A higher-resolution photograph is needed before any further work.

identification: Missal, Holy Week: Tuesday, end of the Passion according to Mark (15:43-46); Wednesday, lesson Isaiah 63:5, 7 and gradual Ne avertas (Ps 68:18, 2). Use not determined
note: Sixteen line beginnings on the recto fall in order on Mark 15:43-46 and sixteen line ends on the verso on Isaiah 63:5 and 7 (without verse 6, as in missals) followed at once by the gradual Ne avertas with verse Salvum me fac. This is a substantial catalogue refinement: the catalogue already named Mark 15:43-46 and Psalm 68; the missal identification, the two days, the Isaiah lesson and the precise gradual are new. The complete book's plenary format is not established by the strip. A research reader reread every line on the native images and compared them with the OCR text of the Arbuthnott missal (1864), pp. 133-134, and with a Google Books snippet of a Lateran missal edition. The manuscript has omnibus que where Arbuthnott prints super omnia quae; Arbuthnott is a witness of the common formulary, not the fragment's use. The use is not determined, the rubric after the Passion is not securely read, and no manuscript missal was collated.

identification: Lemmatic commentary on the marriage section of the verse Summula de Summa Raymundi (Magister Adam); not the commentary printed with the poem nor the apparatus of Kiel Cod. ms. Bord. 37; the commentary itself unidentified
note: The catalogue's "unidentified theological treatise" is a 14th-century lemmatic commentary on the marriage section of the verse Summula de Summa Raymundi (Magister Adam); three textura lemmata and a paraphrased passage match the poem in order, now checked on page images of the Cologne print (MDZ bsb00040641, scans 136, 142, 165). The commentary is not the printed one, nor the 1360 apparatus in Kiel Cod. ms. Bord. 37, which agrees with the print at "Legittime iungi" where the fragment divides and words the passage differently. Other Summula commentaries (Clm 4633, Wolfenbüttel 626 Helmst., Düsseldorf B 181) were not tested, and no heading or explicit survives on the fragment, so the result stays partial. Two strips carry an unrelated, unidentified rhymed text in praise of a virgin on their other face.

identification: Four strips of a two-column manuscript with underlined lemmata and sigla, perhaps a canon-law commentary; no connected phrase survives
note: Four binding strips from a two-column, late 13th-century manuscript; only two lines on strip C and five on strip D give whole words, the rest is line edges or abraded shadow. Underlined lemmata and abbreviated allegations (one read as De cons. di.) point to a canon-law commentary, but no connected phrase survives to search and no candidate was tested. Not identified; better imaging of the abraded faces is what would reopen it.

identification: Trimmed leaf abraded to a few letter stubs; no connected text
note: Both faces examined at native size. The recto keeps one word-ending (]ribus), a few letter stubs at the torn left edge, and six isolated barred as that look like printing set-off; the verso has no writing. No connected text survives in the published images, so no search was run. Not identified; better imaging would be needed.

identification: Gutter strip with the ends of one column's lines and the beginnings of the next; no two consecutive words survive
note: Both faces examined; only the outer few letters of each line survive on either side of a blank gutter band, about 25 lines a face. No two consecutive words can be read, so no search was run and no candidate exists. Not identified; sibling strips from the same binding would be needed.

identification: Strip of a cursive leaf reused as a printer's frisket; short entries ending in 'f.' and a number suggest a table with folio references; no connected words
note: Not identified. A narrow strip from an English cursive leaf of the later 14th century, reused as a printer's frisket and overlaid with red printing ink; only letter groups are legible on either face. Entries are short and several end in "f." plus an arabic number (32, 129), which suggests a table with folio references, but no connected words were obtained and no search could be made. Better imaging (UV or multispectral) is what would reopen it.

catalogue_title: Unidentified text | with offset of other text
identification: Top five lines of a two-column leaf in a small abbreviated hand with glosses, naming Stephen and Luke; not the Legenda aurea; no source found
note: Still not identified. The Legenda aurea (Stephen, Inventio S. Stephani, Luke) was searched in Graesse's text and does not contain the recto wording; searches for a Gamaliel/Lucianus or Cornelius vision passage with these words also found nothing. The first word of the recto is a truncated name ending "-nel/-liel", unresolved. A macro image is still needed.

identification: Scrap with two to five letters at the edge of seven or eight lines a face; no complete word secure
note: A 3.5 x 5.5 cm scrap with a margin and the first or last two to five letters of seven or eight lines of a large 14th-century textualis, one red capital. No word is complete and nothing is searchable; a mechanical test of the line-end letters against the Vulgate found no fit. Not identified, and not resolvable from this scrap alone.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 8/7
identification: Nine line ends of an abbreviated cursive, perhaps scholastic or legal; no three consecutive words secure
note: Nine line-ends of a heavily abbreviated late fourteenth-century cursive; the verso is blank. No sequence of three words can be read securely, so nothing was searched and no candidate exists. Not identified; the page looks scholastic or legal in character but that is description only.

identification: Three paper scraps: one citing Gratian's De consecratione, one with a red heading and short narrative phrases, one illegible; no source found
note: Three paper scraps in at least two hands. Fragment [1] cites "de consecratione dist." (Gratian) beside a second column or gloss; fragment [2] has a red heading ending "iij" and the pieces "-ndebat(ur) in tem-", "et quoddam mir-", "-turo fue-", "ad specu-"; fragment [3] is illegible. Searches on guessed completions of fragment [2] in Google Books, Internet Archive, Corpus Corporum and MDZ found nothing. Not identified.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 11/7 bis
identification: Four paper scraps in at least two hands; no two consecutive secure words
note: Four paper scraps of at most 18 x 9 mm written surface, from at least two hands; all seven images were read at native size. No two consecutive secure words survive on any scrap, so no search was run.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 19/7
identification: Paper scrap of about two centimetres with three line ends and four line beginnings; isolated words only
note: A 2 cm paper scrap with three line-ends on one face and four line-beginnings on the other, in an early fifteenth-century cursive. The only fairly secure words are "color", "[m]ale" and "gula(m)". No connected text survives, so nothing was searched. Not identified.

identification: Two spine strips with line ends of three to eight letters and a numbered section (319); perhaps a legal work in numbered sections; no phrase to search
note: Not identified. Two spine strips in situ show only line-ends of a few letters; no connected phrase can be read and no search was possible. The letter groups look like civil-law allegations, which with the catalogue's leaf numbers 155 and 148/158 and marginal section number 319 suggests a long legal work in numbered sections, untested. Reopen if the strips are lifted or imaged by multispectral light, especially the text beside the red initial I.

catalogue_title: Unidentified glosses on a legal text (?)
identification: Spine strips exposed as a band about ten millimetres wide, one or two common words a line; no connected phrase; the legal character suggested by the catalogue not confirmed
note: Not identified. The strips are exposed only as a 10 mm band in the gutter, giving one or two common words a line ("ieiuni-", "operis", "dominus est", "tali tradi-") and no connected phrase; three proximity searches found nothing and carry no weight. The catalogue's "glosses on a legal text (?)" is not confirmed by the words legible in the images, which have no legal citation forms. Reopen if the strips are lifted or better imaged.

identification: Psalter text, Psalm 49:5-10 (Gallican or Roman wording) on the strip in the "ant" images; the second strip probably Psalm 49:15-20. Kind of book open (psalter, breviary or Bible)
note: On the strip shown in the "ant" images seven consecutive line fragments fall on Psalm 49:5-10 in order at one-line intervals of 33 to 40 letters, with coloured initials on the verse openings Et, Audi and Non. The strip in the "post" images is only probably Psalm 49:15-20, on "]ero od[", "]um S" one line later and a red stroke where Peccatori would stand. A research reader reread every line on the native images and compared them with an online transcription of the Stuttgart Vulgate, not a page image. The readings iumenta and holocau- exclude the version from the Hebrew; Gallican and Roman wording cannot be separated. The kind of book (psalter, breviary or Bible) is open, and the hidden sides and the two covered strips were not seen. Even if the second strip's proposed text is correct, placement of the two strips in one column is compatible with the text sequence but unproved.

identification: Four spine strips with two- and three-word line middles ('loco statuit', 'seductores', 'propugnator-'); not Augustine's De civitate Dei; no source found
note: Not identified. Four spine strips in situ give only cut two- and three-word line-middles (clearest: "loco statuit / omnes ... / seu centum / uirginitatem(?)"; also "seductores", "propugnator-", blue initial "Quem"). The vocabulary does not look philosophical, but no candidate text was found; De civitate Dei was checked against the full text and excluded. Needs a flat, in-focus image of the strip with the red "Post" initial.

identification: Eberhard of Béthune, Graecismus, XIX 118-121 (lower strip, Frammento 3, only; upper strip unidentified)
note: The four lines of the lower strip are the middles of four consecutive verses of Graecismus XIX 118-121 (ex se reliq-, orno como s-, -das huic quoque s-, -es dicas gale-) and show no difference from Wrobel's text in the surviving letters. A research reader reread all lines on enlarged crops of canvas 2 and compared the lower strip with the OCR text of the archive.org scan of Wrobel's edition, not with the page image. Verse 118 has ex se, where the apparatus records in se for one manuscript (P); the other recorded variant places are mostly outside the strip. The upper strip (Frammento 2), in a small cursive with scholastic vocabulary, is unidentified: that it is commentary on the Graecismus is a guess, and whether the two strips are one leaf is open. Only a slice about 23 mm wide of each strip is visible and no manuscript of the Graecismus was collated.

institution: Aarschot, Archief van de collegiale Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekerk
catalogue_title: Glosses to an unidentified scientific text
identification: Marginal glosses to Aristotle, De sensu et sensato, chapter 3 (439b18-440b), probably on William of Moerbeke's translation; not the expositions of Thomas Aquinas or Albert the Great; the gloss itself unidentified
note: The strip is the cut-off margin of a leaf of Aristotle's De sensu et sensato with summary glosses to chapter 3 (439b18-440b); no main text survives. The locus is confirmed by sequence and technical terms against William of Moerbeke's translation as printed in the Leonine edition (OCR text), and the gloss's "defluxionem" and "superpositus" lean towards that version rather than the older one, which was not read. The gloss was compared with Thomas Aquinas and Albert the Great in full for this passage and with extracts of Adam of Buckfield and Alexander of Aphrodisias quoted in the Leonine apparatus; it shares their articulation but none of their wording. Result stays partial: glossed text identified, gloss unidentified.

identification: Strip with the first three to six letters of about thirty lines and four red paragraph marks; no complete word secure at the published size
note: Narrow binding strip with only the first few letters of each line on one face and an abraded other face. No complete word can be read at the published resolution, so no search was possible. Unidentified; would need an adjoining strip or better imaging.

identification: Cut edge of a marginal commentary in chancery cursive beside a pen-flourished initial; isolated letter groups only
note: Orientation settled: the opened strip (canvas 2) reads rotated 180 degrees and is direct Latin chancery cursive, not mirrored and not a right-to-left script. What is visible is the cut edge of the marginal commentary; the main text is under the residue band beside the pen-flourished initial. Only isolated letter groups can be read, so nothing was searchable and the text stays unidentified. A legal gloss is a guess, not a finding.

identification: Lenten sermons on the weekday Mass readings (Friday and Saturday after Ash Wednesday, Saturday of the second week), apparently for religious; collection unidentified
note: The four leaves are Lenten sermons on the daily Mass readings, not a theological treatise. They cover the Friday and Saturday after Ash Wednesday (Matt. 5:43ff., Mark 6:47ff.) and the Saturday of the second week (Gen. 27, Luke 15). The Saturday material reads religio as the ship and draws on Simon's tomb with its sculpted ships (1 Macc. 13). Jacobus de Voragine's quadragesimale and Hugo de Prato Florido's de tempore sermons were compared and do not match; the collection is unidentified.

identification: Moral compilation using medical similes (fasting, vanity of life, penance, confessor as physician); draws on Johannes de S. Geminiano, Summa de exemplis II, and shares text with Rainerius de Pisis, Pantheologia, Poenitentia c. XX; containing work unidentified
note: The five Gent leaves are a late fourteenth-century Latin moral compilation, not a medical treatise. Its chapters treat fasting, the vanity of human life, penance as the tending of a vine, and the confessor as a physician of souls. The river simile on fols. [1]v-[2]r reworks Johannes de Sancto Geminiano, Summa de exemplis II, closely. The physician-confessor chapters share long verbatim runs with Rainerius de Pisis, Pantheologia, s.v. Poenitentia c. XX, but are fuller and ordered differently. The containing work is unidentified.

identification: Ink too faint for connected text at the published size
note: These are two foxed paper leaves in a faint 15th-century cursiva, two columns, Latin theological prose. Only isolated words could be read (anima, gratia tripla, filius dei, misericordia, a possible "Beleth/Beda cap. xi" citation), which is not enough for a phrase search. The text is unidentified; better imaging is the precondition for further work.

identification: Scraped logic text legible only as isolated terms under UV
note: Scraped 14th-century two-column cover from Orselina, legible in UV only as isolated words: propositio, affirmativa/negativa, species, diffinitio, finita/infinita, and a red-paraphed "Contra". The genre looks like scholastic logic (Topics or Peri hermeneias material), but no connected phrase could be read, so nothing was searchable or comparable. Unidentified; it needs better imaging or reading at the object.

catalogue_title: Unidentified glosses on a legal text
identification: Legal text and gloss visible only as a few letters per line through a paper strip
note: Spine-reinforcement leaf of a 14th-century Italian glossed legal text, almost entirely covered by a paper strip. At the published resolution only 5-8 letters per line are exposed, and they could not be read to word level, even in blue-channel enhanced crops. The catalogue's own Wood's-lamp readings (Iur-, Mulieres) could not be checked on the images. No identification was attempted beyond listing the canon-law chapters that open with Mulieres; UV imaging or lifting the paper strip is needed.

identification: Questions on the origin and practice of confession; same object as part of F-ho7z; work unidentified
note: Not identified. These three linings are the 45 Da 5 half of the virtual reconstruction F-ho7z, so they belong with it by definition. Rereading the lower strip shows a sequence on how confession originates: from Christ's order at the raising of Lazarus, from a medical argument about disclosing a disease, and from James 5:16. Further searches, including inside Johannes Andreae's Novella on Omnis utriusque, found no text with this wording.

identification: Sermon or exposition material on Mary Magdalene and Jacob typology, probably de sanctis; not a psalter commentary
note: Not identified. One face treats Mary Magdalene through the topos of Christ defending the silent Mary against the murmuring Pharisee and the complaining Martha. The other face expounds Jacob (Esau the hunter as the devil, the stolen blessing, the wrestling with the angel) and probably applies it to the apostle James. The Psalm 9:30 verse is a cross-reference, not the base text. The Magdalene-then-James order suggests sermons or expositions de sanctis, but no text with this wording was found. Jacobus de Voragine's Sermones de sanctis and the Legenda aurea were read for both feasts and do not match.

identification: Six faded partial lines; nothing searchable at the published size
note: Not identified. Six faded partial lines in a small textualis currens with red capital strokes; the other face shows no legible text. The script, decoration and line spacing differ from Fragm. 331 a (F-2nxm), so the two strips come from different manuscripts despite the shared binding. Too little is legible for a phrase search; multispectral imaging would be needed.

identification: Scholastic question on whether complexio is the form of the body; work unidentified
note: The fragment is a 13th- or 15th-century scholastic question (the catalogue conflicts) on whether complexio is the form of the complexioned body ("forma complexionati corporis") or an accidental disposition. It has a Sed contra and replies Ad primum, Ad secundum, Ad tertium, and only one column block of the bifolium is legible at the published resolution. Phrase searches found only doctrinal parallels (Bonaventure, Albert, Aquinas SCG II.63, Taddeo Alderotti), no matching text. It stays unresolved pending better images.

catalogue_title: Subject index to unidentified theological texts on virtues and vices
identification: Subject index on virtues, vices and other topics referring to numbered items and to 'Godefridus' and 'Remundus'; indexed works unidentified
note: This is a 14th-century subject index (tabula) with "Q(ue)re n(umer)o" references to a numbered collection. It also sends readers to "Godefridus" (for the seven deadly sins and their contrary virtues, the ten commandments and penance) and to "Remundus" (penance, presumably Raymond of Peñafort). Its subjects range from theology and canon law to lapidary lore and the seven imperial electors, so the numbers probably denote items or volumes, not chapters of one work. Goffredus de Trano's Summa was checked in OCR and does not contain the vices septenary. Main work and Godefridus remain unidentified.

identification: Moral treatise on avarice quoting Seneca, Jerome Ep. 71 and Ambrose; containing work unidentified
note: The strip is a discursive Latin treatment of avarice that paraphrases and glosses its authorities: Jerome Ep. 71, Seneca NQ V.15, Epp. 94, 119 and 90, and Ambrose In Ps. 118 and De off. III.7. The catalogue's "Ep. 109" is Ep. 119.12. Manipulus florum and Trevet on Boethius II m.5 were checked and excluded. On OCR, Peraldus De avaritia shares the opening "ad pedes apostolorum" topos but with different authorities, Bromyard has Ep. 119 and the Ambrose line only in other articles and contexts, and the Communiloquium (poor OCR) has none of the quotations. The containing work is unidentified.

identification: Strips with two to four cut lines per column; too sparse to identify
note: The two 14th-century headband strips keep only 2-4 cut lines per column. A red rubric ending paula/pauli introducing a new item is the main lead. Legenda aurea De sancta Paula was tested and does not collate in the second column. Aquinas on 1 Timothy was also rejected. The strips are too sparse to identify without better imaging.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
identification: Only ghosts of a large script on a stained paper leaf
note: A stained paper part-leaf with ghosts of a large textura. The only dark-ink group reads something like "...nnia et" and may be an offset. Nothing searchable in ordinary photographs; unidentified.

identification: One main-hand line end fits the Lauds antiphon Trium puerorum (Cantus 005191); not confirmed
note: The strip's one surviving line in the main hand ends ... benedicentes d(omi)n(u)m. This fits the Lauds antiphon Trium puerorum (CAO 5191), but the preceding and following words are too trimmed to confirm it. The two cursive lines below are unidentified.

identification: No main text above the seam; marginal allegations suggest Gratian's Decretum, part II
note: Binding strip with only a blue/red running head ("...A . Q(?) . VII") and later marginal allegations in canon-law form (causa/quaestio references and chapter incipits). Its text block is trimmed off. The lower flap with large textura belongs to F-815q. Nothing searchable; unidentified.

identification: Two or three washed-out lines; nothing searchable
note: A narrow bifolium strip whose 2-3 surviving lines on one face are washed out. Only red paraphs, a red "...nio" and later pen trials are clear. Ordinary photographs give no searchable text; unidentified, and UV imaging would be needed.

catalogue_title: Law compilation | Unidentified legal text (fol. [1]r); Carta de foresta, art. 9-11 (fol. [1]v)
identification: Fol. [1]r is a canon-law list of penal cases citing the Liber Extra (X 5.38.13 Cum infirmitas, X 5.6, X 5.17), probably from an English pastoral manual of the Oculus sacerdotis / Pupilla oculi kind that pairs such lists with the Carta de foresta; the list itself is unidentified
note: Fol. [1]r is a canon-law list of penal cases, each with a Liber Extra citation; it is not a statute. One entry paraphrases X 5.38.13 Cum infirmitas ("Medicus nolens monere et inducere [infir]mum ... [ad]vocet medic[um anim]e ... ex. de [pen. et re. c. Cum in]firmitas"). Nearby are citations "ex. de iudeis ... postulasti" (probably X 5.6.14) and "ex. de raptoribus" (X 5.17). The compiling list is unidentified. The pairing of a case list with the Forest Charter matches English pastoral manuals: Pagula's Oculus sacerdotis (Penn Ms. Codex 721, ff. 50-55) and the Pupilla oculi both embed the Forest Charter among canon-law case lists. But the lists read in both (Penn 721 f. 54v, the satisfaction cases; the Pupilla interdict cases) do not contain the medicus entry.

identification: Johannes Dacus, De gradibus formarum (sophisma), ed. Otto 1955, pp. 554-555 and 561
note: The corner of the front pastedown visible under the paper (canvas 0) agrees with Otto's edition p. 561, on the analogy of being and God as the measure of beings, in sequence over parts of ten consecutive lines (2-11), with variants; line 1 remains illegible; the joint line (canvas 11) agrees with pp. 554-555 ('primum substans est materia prima; nam quicquid substat'). A research reader reread all visible lines on the images; the coordinator read canvas 0 lines 8-11 against the edition. The source text is Google Books snippets of the edition that together cover the collated run; no page image was available. In line 7 the manuscript seems to have one word where the edition reads 'entis. Sed substantie' (unresolved), line 8 appears to read 'quia ens quod est sub[...]' rather than the edition's 'propter' (continuation unresolved), and the manuscript lacks the bracketed 'non' in the edition snippets (editorial convention unchecked). The catalogue's 'Commentary to Aristotle's Metaphysics (?)' was a genre guess; the fragment is not claimed as a new witness.

identification: Quotes Regula Benedicti 6.1 under a heading on silence; containing work unidentified
note: The legible lines quote Regula Benedicti 6.1 ("Faciamus quod ait propheta: Dixi custodiam vias meas [ut non delinquam]"), introduced by "De silencio dicit vir sanctus in regula". The containing work, a later text citing the Rule under a heading on silence, is unidentified. A separate German piece on the same back pastedown is not part of this record's description.

identification: Gilbert the Universal, Glossa ordinaria in Lamentationes, book I, on Lam. 1:16 and 1:17
note: Two in-situ spine tabs carry line ends from the Glossa ordinaria on Lamentations. Tab B is on 1:16 ('[docto]rum ecclesiam s(ibi) c[ommissam] ... fonte a[moris] ... [la]crimas p(ro)ducat') and tab A is on 1:17 Allegorice ('[q]ua p(ossi)t hostium / uince(re) & sua defende(re) / polluta fed[i]t[at]e car[nalium] ... hostes q(uibus)'). A research reader compared all seven visible lines with the Lyon 1545 Glossa page images (scans 392-393) and with snippets of Andree's edition (pp. 256, 260); the coordinator checked tab A lines 1-2 against scan 393. The wording follows the Glossa, not its source Paschasius ('hostes revincere, suaque defendere dogmata'). Martin of Leon, who reuses the 1:16 sentence, was not found to contain the 1:17 passage, a result that rests on MDZ OCR and the PL text only and weakens this alternative without conclusively excluding it. Andree's apparatus was not seen; the opening words of tab A l. 4 and tab B l. 2 are uncertain; F-dkld is a different volume.

identification: Imaged face carries only a painted initial
note: The only imaged face of the Cod. 3569 fragment is a 110 mm painted initial A with acanthus ornament and a later shelfmark; it carries no text. The adjacent text leaf belongs to the host. Unidentified; the hidden face, if any text survives, needs imaging.

identification: Abraded dorsal patch; no searchable text
note: The dorsal patch at the head of the wrapper's spine shows six or seven abraded lines on each side of a later spine strip. At the published resolution only isolated letters ("omne"?) can be made out, so nothing could be searched. The two-column Euphrosyne text in the first reading belongs to the wrapper bifolium, which is a sibling record, not to this one.

identification: Erased lower text unreadable in the published images; the legible table indexes the host volume
note: The legible red-and-black list on both pastedowns of Cod. 1695 is a table of contents to the host's own sermons (a1-e9, ending "In cena domini ... Finis tabule"), matching the host's lost opening, final sermon and 92 leaves; the catalogue already said so. The catalogued fragment is the erased German text beneath, which is not legible in the published visible-light images. Unidentified; UV imaging needed.

catalogue_title: Unidentified religious treatise in Anglo-Norman verse
identification: Marcus, Visio Tnugdali (Vision of Tundale), Anglo-Norman translation in octosyllabic couplets, Lucifer to the field of joy (ed. Wagner 1882, pp. 36-41)
note: The two leaves translate, in the Latin's order, the Visio Tnugdali from the description of Lucifer to the gate and field of joy with the fount of life, phrase by phrase and in sequence on all four faces. A research reader compared the reread columns with Wagner's 1882 edition, using page images for pp. 36, 38 and 41. The coordinator found phrase-by-phrase correspondence for canvas 3, col b, box 760,340-1420,1200, against p. 41 lines 2-8. The identification is of the work translated: no edition of this French text was found, so it was compared with the Latin. The translation is free and amplifying (especially on prelates), is in octosyllabic couplets, and differs in form from the edited Dublin TCD 312 alexandrine version. It is not recorded in the sources checked (ARLIMA, Easting 1997, Gardiner 1993, Picard 1989). Dean and Boulton 1999, Palmer 1982, Cavagna 2017 and Jonas were unavailable, and no novelty is claimed.

institution: Chicago, University of Chicago Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center
identification: Commentary on the Apocalypse, Apoc 5:1-8 and 6:10-15, reading the seals as seven status of the Church; not Hugh of St Cher, Vitalis, Berengaudus, Olivi or Joachim; work unidentified
note: F-1tv3 is a continuous lemma commentary on Apoc 5:1-8 and 6:10-15 that reads the seals as seven status ecclesie, the sixth running from the coming of Antichrist to his death. The "top" and "bottom" strips are the middle and foot of the same two leaves, against the catalogue's suggestion of two bifolia. Hugh of St Cher, Vitalis/ps.-Albert, both Corpus Thomisticum commentaries, Joachim, Berengaudus (1554 print, page read), Olivi (OCR snippets of Lewis's transcription) and the PL Apocalypse commentaries (Richard, Haymo, Anselm of Laon, Alexander Minorita and others) were compared at Apoc 6:11-13 and do not match. Lyra and Gorran could not be checked. The work remains unidentified, probably an unedited school commentary.

identification: Literal exposition (divisio and lemma glosses) of Aristotle, De anima II.5-III.1 (417b5 to the opening of Book III at 424b22); not Thomas Aquinas or Giles of Rome; commentator unidentified
note: Literal exposition (divisio, "id est" glosses, "legatur littera sic", "Sciendum" notabilia, no quaestiones) of De anima II.5-6 (417b5-418a24) and II.11 to III.1 (423b29-424b22+). The catalogue's "427b22" is an error for 424b22, the opening of Book III. Compared with Aquinas's Sentencia (Corpus Thomisticum) at three loci and with Giles of Rome's Expositio (1500 print, page images, fol. 35r and 53v): neither matches. The question commentaries are excluded by genre, and the 1240s anonymous expositions (Bazán 1998, Gauthier 1985) were not accessible, so the commentator remains unidentified.

catalogue_title: Legendary | Miracles of St James and saints' lives of St Clement and St Eustace
identification: Anonymous preaching compilation of exempla in 20 chapters (prologue 'In hoc consequenti opusculo ordinantur in certis titulis'), section IV De sanctis, subchapters 1-6 and 34-39 (= Cambridge CCCC MS 327, ff. 175v-176r, 179v-180v)
note: The bifolium agrees in chapter sequence and in the compiler's own wording with section IV of the compilation in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 327: the Gregory framings with the additions 'et estu immenso' and 'vir mirabili gratia dotatus', the false reference 'in xvi libro de sacramentis', and 'fructus vere patientie'. A research reader collated four passages from both faces with the Parker on the Web page images (ff. 175v, 176r, 180r) and checked the sequence through Becket and Giles on ff. 179v and 180v. The coordinator found line-by-line agreement for f. 25v col. b (canvas 1, box 1850,5100-4450,6150) against f. 176r, the rubric between the items differing ('vi cap.' against 'Similis precedenti'). The rubrication differs throughout (Gent numbers chapters within the section, Cambridge across the work, offset 89), and the wording differences are minor. The work is unedited and anonymous; the other recorded copies (Florence BNCF Conv. Soppr. D.8.1128, Les Enluminures TM 427, BL Sloane 4029) were not seen.

identification: Miscellany of excerpts and exempla, including ps.-Augustine, Dialogus quaestionum LXV qq. 15-20, Verba seniorum items and Jacques de Vitry exempla in other wording; collection unidentified
note: Partial (medium). ff. 2ra-rb are Ps.-Augustine, Dialogus quaestionum LXV qq. XV-XX (PL 40), compared in sequence. f. 4r has two Verba seniorum stories and the Ps.-Augustine/Hrabanus Sunday sermon "Sciendum est fratres karissimi". The florilegium on 1v-2v draws on Jerome Ep. 118, Augustine Enarrationes, Gregory Moralia and Cassian Inst. IV.43. The exempla from 4vb are retellings of Jacques de Vitry stock (Crane 114, 215, 256-257), not his wording, and no single known collection matched; the containing compilation is unidentified.

identification: Reworking of William Peraldus, Summa de virtutibus, De dono timoris (rubric 'De speciebus timoris. LXXXIII'); order differs from the print and from Clm 2654; containing work unidentified
note: The leaf carries Peraldus, Summa de virtutibus, De dono timoris: the end of the introduction on 1r, then the chapter De speciebus timoris (rubric "LXXXIII") through Cupiditatem nocendi per te habes on 1v. It agrees in sustained wording and sequence with the 1614 edition, pp. 330-331, and was checked on page images. The chapter is arranged differently from the printed text: there is no Bede/Bernard opening, Bernard's triplex timor comes after filial fear, and the chapter number does not fit Peraldus's divisions. A dated Peraldus manuscript of 1297 (Clm 2654) has the printed order, not the fragment's. So the leaf is recorded as partial: an abridgement or reworking of Peraldus whose own title is not yet identified. The catalogue's comparison with Ripelin's CTV V.39 is a parallel only.

identification: Exposition of Hebrews 11:33-34, clause by clause with literal and moral senses (commentary or martyrs' sermon), not a Job commentary; not Thomas Aquinas or Hugh of St Cher; work unidentified
note: The text is a moral and literal exposition of Hebrews 11:33-34 ("operati sunt iustitiam" through "aciem gladii"), quoting Job 5:7, Heb 13:5 and 13:8, and Isa 54:7. It is not a commentary on Job. Thomas and Hugh of St Cher on the passage do not match, and no edition matched phrase searches. The text order suggests that canvas 1 precedes canvas 0.

institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: Sunday-gospel homily or exposition on Mt 8:23-27 (4th Sunday after Epiphany), then Mt 13:24; cites Bede; collection unidentified
note: Sunday-gospel homily or exposition: the end of the fourth Sunday after Epiphany (Matthew 8:23-27, boat of the cross, ships of the devil, Apocalypse 8:9) and the opening of the fifth (Matthew 13:24) under a red initial. The catalogue's "Beda" is a cited source. The leaf paraphrases Bede, In Lucam/In Marcum on the disciples waking Christ, and shares imagery with Remigius, hom. 9. The containing collection is unidentified, and Voragine's sermons for the day do not match. Both faces were read by the research reader at native size.

identification: Rhythmic poem on St Agnes, 'Mundi orbis gratuletur', followed by colophon verses naming Martinus de Grudencz; not in Analecta Hymnica, Chevalier or Cantus
note: The Agnes poem on 1v ("Mundi orbis gratuletur deum trinum veneretur Agnetis") was not found in AH 1-55 (full-text grep), Chevalier RH, Mone or Cantus; Walther's Initia could not be searched. Its signature verses ("Nomen autoris si tu scrutamine queris / Mar tibi sit primum ...") are a known colophon printed by Feller (1686, p. 448) from a Leipzig Paulina manuscript and discussed in Centralblatt für Bibliothekswesen 11 (1894), no. 36. Martinus de Grudencz is therefore attested as the name in a scribe's colophon, and his authorship of the poem is not established. Partial, low: the genre and subject are clear, but the text is unprinted as far as checked.

identification: Latin moral or homiletic prose on tears and lamentation (cites John 11, Apoc 8:13, Lam 1), not medical; work unidentified
note: The catalogue's "possibly medical" is wrong. The strips carry Latin homiletic or moral prose on weeping: Christ's tears at Lazarus (Jo. 11), the "Vae, vae, vae" of Apoc. 8:13 glossed as sins of heart, mouth and deed, the gift of tears, "rain scatters a great wind", Lam. 1:12. The topics overlap Fasciculus morum and the Legenda aurea, but no wording was matched. The work is unidentified; the genre is the only result.

catalogue_title: Bible commentary | Possibly a commentary on John 12
identification: Sermon on the day's gospel, John 12:20-32, with Jer 46:12 ('fortis impegit in fortem'), probably Passiontide; not Voragine's Quadragesimale; collection unidentified
note: Face 1 is a homiletic exposition of John 12:20-32, described as "the gospel of the day" ("in euangelio hodierno"). It quotes 12:24, 12:26 and 12:32, and is preceded by a rubricated Jer 46:12 ("fortis impegit in fortem ... pariter conciderunt"). It looks like a Passiontide sermon, not a commentary. Jacobus de Voragine's Quadragesimale and Durand's Rationale were checked and do not match. Face 2 is too abraded to read.

shelfmark: Archief van Sint-Baafs en bisdom Gent, SN 196
identification: Compact commentary or summa on Gratian's Decretum (D.1, D.4, D.6, C.27 qq. 1-2); not Rufinus, Paucapalea, Rolandus or Bernard of Pavia; work unidentified
note: Two quire-guard strips carry a compact commentary or summa on Gratian's Decretum, not a theological treatise. The datable passages fall at D.1 (a "mos" diagram: scripta/constitutio, non scripta/consuetudo; "humanum genus duobus regitur"), D.4 ("quod principi placuit legis habet vigorem"), D.6 d.p.c.3 ("figurativa ... superficiem ... misterium") and C.27 qq.1-2 ("voto annexum", "licentiam transfretandi", "uxori suadeat"). Rufinus, Paucapalea, Rolandus and Bernard of Pavia do not contain the wording. Goffredus could not be searched, and the containing summa is unidentified. All exposed lines were read by the research reader; canvas 2's exposed strip is blank.

catalogue_title: Commentarium super Petri Hispani summulas logicales
identification: Literal commentary on Peter of Spain, divisio textus on Tracts IX-XI (de Rijk 1972 numbering); front strip close to the anonymous Compilationes supra Summulas Petri Hispani ('Omnes homines') in Nuremberg GNM Hs 27773; the work is not established
note: The front strip follows the Compilationes' divisio of Tracts IX-X in Nuremberg GNM Hs 27773, fol. 128ra, clause by clause but not verbatim: it adds 'quia opposita iuxta se posita magis elucescunt' and reads 'explanat' for 'exponit'. The back strip shares only the structure of the Tract XI outline. Literal commentaries on the Summulae borrow from one another without acknowledgement, so this is a source connection, not an identification of the work. A Fragmentarium editor reviewed it in October 2026: front-strip parallels strong but imperfect, back strip without the same lemmata. Only one witness was compared; Vienna ÖNB Cod. 2389, reported by de Rijk as interpolated, could help settle the relation (manuscripta.at was down at the time of review). Stopped pending that witness.

catalogue_title: Prophecy in Old French | for an unknown year
identification: Old French (Picard) version, for one year, of the Tuesday entry of the January kalends prognostic, Latin in ps.-Bede, Pronostica temporum (PL 90, 951-952); no French source text found
note: The slip is a Picard rendering, for a single year (awan, "this year"), of the Tuesday entry of the Latin Kalends-of-January prognostic (Si tertia feria [fuerint kal. Ian.], hiems umbrosa/imbrosa ... naves periclitabuntur et reges peribunt; Ps.-Bede, Pronostica temporum, PL 90, 951-952). All six clauses correspond in order. Nees perilleront means "ships will be imperilled", not "children will die". The French wording was not found in print, so this is a source identification (partial, medium).

identification: Prose abridgement of Priscian, Institutiones V (gender by final syllable, GL II 145-164); the abridgement is unidentified
note: The two text columns on 25r-v are a prose abridgement of Priscian, Institutiones V (noun genders by final syllable, GL II c. 145-164). Collation shows Priscian's rules, exception lists and connecting wording, with the citations stripped, recast as "Omnia nomina in -X desinentia..." regulae with "In AR./In AS./In ES./In US./In IS." cues. The specific abridgement is unidentified: it is not Papias, Alcuin or Petrus Helias as quoted by Vincent, and the Glosule and the Excerptiones de Prisciano remain untested. 26r has only a later pricing note; 26v is blank.

catalogue_title: Unidentified text, possibly by Johannes Chrysostomos | Possibly De reparatione lapsi
identification: Rubric marks the end of John Chrysostom, De reparatione lapsi (Latin), and the start of a further Chrysostom work; main text too abraded to collate
note: The red rubric on canvas 1 reads "[Explicit ... Jo]hannis Crisostomi de reparacione [lapsi ... li]ber primus eiusdem de p[s]almo(?)". It marks the end of Chrysostom's Latin De reparatione lapsi and the start of another Chrysostom work, which supports the catalogue's guess. The brown text is blurred, and with both faces showing through each other none of it could be read or collated, so the identification of the body text is unconfirmed. Status partial, pending better imaging.

identification: Middle Dutch devotional prose, apparently a thanksgiving prayer echoing Anselm's 'gratias ago quia creasti in me imaginem tuam'; no source found
note: F-6zm1 (two narrow strips, about six lines) carries a Middle Dutch prayer-like text. It reads "...god na minen cleynen vermoch[...] / dattu my hebste ghemaket na d[inen beelde]...", a thanksgiving motif close to Anselm's gratias ago quia creasti in me imaginem tuam. Searches of CMNL, DBNL, Google Books and IA found no source with this wording. Busch's thanksgiving prayer and the Dutch Soliloquium were checked and rejected. Unidentified.

identification: Hippocrates, Regimen acutorum, book IV with Galen's commentary (Latin), Textus XIX-XX and XXIV-XXVII (Giunta 1527 numbering)
note: The red text is the Hippocratic lemma and the black is Galen's commentary. Face A carries the end of Textus XIX and the start of XX, and face B the end of the commentary on XXIV and Textus XXV-XXVII. A research reader compared XIX, XX, XXV and XXVII with page images of the Venice 1527 Giunta edition (MDZ bsb10139648, scans 709-712), and the coordinator found line-by-line agreement for Textus XXVII (canvas 1, box 600,2780-1480,3500, against scan 712). In XIX the manuscript reads 'sed ab assumpt[ione]' where the edition has 'sed ad defectionem'. The translator was not checked, no claim is made about the Latin version or print tradition, and the abraded mid-face commentary was not compared.

identification: Breviary chapter readings: Jer 23:6-7 with rubric 'Ad .ix. cap.' and Phil 1:7; office and use unidentified
note: Two strips of F-oc1a join vertically on both faces. They carry Jer 23:6 followed by the rubric "Ad .ix. cap." and a None chapter beginning "[P]ropter hoc" (probably Jer 23:7), and on the other face Phil 1:7. The leaf is therefore from an Office book (breviary or capitulary) with chapters, not a Bible. Day, use and book type remain open.

identification: Latin commentary strip with red-underlined lemmata; too faint at the available resolution to fix the lemma
note: Faint strip with native images of only about 15 px/mm. The red-underlined lemma may read "[ne] nos inducas" (Pater noster), but the reading is insecure and no source was compared. It stays unidentified pending better images.

identification: Offset of a two-column civil-law Codex lectura, probably on C. 6.43.3 (Communia de legatis, l. ult.) with the Authentica Res quae subiacent; not the Accursian gloss, Bartolus or the 1519 lectura printed as Bellapertica; commentator unidentified
note: Mirror-image offsets on both boards of a two-column 14th-century civil-law Codex commentary (ff./C. allegations only; first-person lectura style, not a glossed text). The lower board discusses fideicommissary restitution, alienation, usucapion and 30-year prescription, eviction in duplum, and pledging. This is the content of C. 6.43.3 and Auth. Res quae subiacent, which is therefore the probable locus. The same discussion is in the 1519 Bellapertica Codex lectura, but the fragment's wording did not match it, so the commentator remains unidentified.

identification: The catalogued object, a 16th-century music fragment in white mensural notation, is not identified and was not attempted. The uncatalogued parchment cover leaf and strip of the same volume are a Mass book, probably a plenary missal: Feria II post Invocavit (Ez 34:11-14, Mt 25:31-35; turn-in Mt 25:46 and Is 55:6) and Feria II post Reminiscere (Jn 8:22-24)
note: The record was catalogued by a project that described only fragments with musical notation, so F-v7a4 is the music fragment; the missal leaf has no catalogue record, as a Fragmentarium editor confirmed in October 2026. The work on the missal leaf stands as a note on the host volume: a research reader collated 39 lines with page images of the 1519 Teutonic Order missal (fols. XXVII, XXXIIII), and the coordinator checked canvas 1 col. b lines 1-5 and the placement on scan 91. The music fragment is open.

identification: Chancery-style letter collection or formulary on six imaged guards ('marchioni montis ferrati', 'post labores studentibus conferuntur'); Petrus de Vinea, Thomas of Capua, Guido Faba, Rockinger's formularies tested without a match; 23 guards not imaged
note: Cod. 3664 guards: about 2-3 lines per strip in a two-column hybrid hand. They mix a Montferrat salutation, a petition formula and a royal "nostre maiestatis" passage on students with penitential and theological wording. Petrus de Vinea (1566 vulgate), Thomas of Capua (MGH 2011) and three Austrian/German formularies were checked and gave no match. Still unidentified; possibly a dictamen or letter collection, as the catalogue already suggested.

identification: Noted breviary, two consecutive Sundays after Pentecost (Iv-IIr strip): antiphon Erat quidam regulus (CAO 2661), collect Familiam tuam, chapters from Eph 6:10-16; then homily lessons from Jerome, In Matthaeum III on Mt 18:23-35, chapter Phil 1:6 and antiphon Dixit autem dominus servo (CAO 2274). IIv homily on Mt 22:15-22 (unscanned) and the unnotated Jn 17 strip remain unidentified
note: Lead from a CoMMA manuscript-text search (tools/comma.py), checked on page images. A research reader (Claude) read the lower strip of both images at native resolution; the two images show one continuous band of the opened bifolium, the right text block split across them. The IIr lines (cuius uxorem et filios uenundatos perseuerante illo in malitia ... nec ecclesiastice interpretationis est nec a prudentibus uiris rec[ipiend..]) were collated on the page image of BnF lat. 17991 (breviary, 12th c.), f. 147v col. b, and with Jerome's text in PL 26 via Corpus Corporum. They agree with both, sharing with lat. 17991 the readings uenundatos and sic et uxorem against PL uenundandos; lat. 17991 puts a lesson break after intelligi uolunt and runs the lesson to non dimittentur, while here the lesson ends at recipiend[..] and the chapter follows on the next line. Chants were checked in Cantus Index; the regulus and Dixit autem antiphons belong to consecutive Sundays, and lat. 17991 f. 148r has Dixit autem as the gospel antiphon after the same homily. The collect and the Eph 6 chapters sit with the regulus antiphon, not with Mt 18 as in the Roman Missal; this hints at the use but was not tested against other books. The Lille 814 and Cambrai 528 HTR hits were not checked on images. The status stays partial: the IIv homily is known only from the catalogue transcription (it follows Jerome and argues like the Heiric-attributed PL 95 homily, Hom. CXCIV, but not in its wording), and the unnotated strip at the top seam (Jn 17:7-8, red rubric [..]e ascensione domini) still points only to a Mass book of the Ascension season.

identification: Offset on a spine of Latin scholastic prose in Italian textualis; the 1642 px photograph gives only scattered words, no connected run to search
note: The fragments are offsets from four parchment spine linings, upside-down mirror images that read correctly after a vertical flip. They show a few words per line of 14th-c. Italian Latin prose, probably scholastic: repellit, intrinseco, existit, veniat, praeter, quod possit, solo alio, immediate, ut tho.. No connected phrase could be read from the single low-resolution photograph, and searches on the surviving words found nothing. The text remains unidentified pending higher-resolution imaging.

identification: Same photograph as F-x33a (Cod. 3588 back board); its German tab has about fifteen cut words, too few to search; the Latin tab is the Rule of Benedict 6.1 passage already recorded under F-x33a
note: F-isvn and F-x33a publish the same photograph of the back-board spine linings of Cod. 3588. F-isvn's catalogued German fragment is the tab below the third cord, partly under the turn-in. Its five cut lines ("Item frem[d..] / das man k.. / vnd das er da.. / vnd darumb ..") are too short to identify. The Latin tab quoting Regula Benedicti 6.1 belongs to F-x33a, and nothing visible shows whether the two tabs come from one manuscript.

institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: Recto too faint for connected text; what is legible looks like further pen trials and notes (a repeated heading 'De bea[ta] ma[ria]?'), not book text
note: The recto of F-722c could not be read connectedly even with contrast enhancement. No candidate was tested. The heading formula "De bea[ta] ma[ria]? / et q(ui) l..." occurs twice (top right, and lower left at y≈1530), and short entries "Me bene ..." repeat in a ruled box. So the recto too looks like notes or pen trials rather than the end of a theological text.

identification: Spine strip F2 keeps only line-ends of one column and first letters of the next; F1 unreadable; the red-Q piece in the photographs belongs to sibling F-0df1
note: F-3d30's strip F2 keeps only the ends of 10-11 lines of column A and the first letters of column B (ff/fo/s/te/r/a). F1 is not readable in any image. The other strips in the photographs are F3/F4 of sibling record F-0df1 (F4 = Psalm 63, the red-Q textualis). Proximity searches on the few secure words (aliquando, vacat qualiter, pro principi, celebri) gave no usable lead.

identification: Office lectionary strips (later marginal 'l. i, iii, iiii'), 1-2 words a line; ordered line-end searches against the Vulgate found nothing; homiliary texts untested
note: Two 12th-century gutter strips keep only one to eight letters a line. Later marginal l(ectio) i / iii / iiii notes show that the text was read in Office lessons. Ordered line-end and line-beginning chains against the Vulgate, and proximity searches in Corpus Corporum, gave no candidate. The fragment is left unidentified; homiliary and legendary corpora remain untested.

identification: Not identified

identification: Copy sheet of three documents of the 1446-1451 Tyrolean settlement: Frederick III's pardon of the Tyrolean estates (Vienna, 2 April 1446), Albrecht VI's parallel pardon (1446, dating clause lost), and Duke Sigmund's confirmation of the Tyrolean liberties (Innsbruck, 17 August 1451)
note: Regests read on the image (01v); document 1 agrees with Chmel, Regesta Friderici III, Anhang 65, and document 3 with Chmel, Materialien I/2 no. CLXXIV, pp. 354-355; document 2 matches Schober no. 17 and RI XIV/4 on issuer and action.
